Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Vignette:
Adaeze Okonkwo, a 54-year-old judge in a busy metropolitan court, had spent decades building a reputation for calm authority. But the memories of what happened during a judicial training mission abroad, nearly four years ago now, refused to stay in the past. She had been detained by a faction of armed men who accused her of collaborating with opposition leaders. They held her in a windowless room for three days. What she remembered came in jagged shards: the cool concrete against her back, the sting of coarse rope around her wrists and ankles, the sour-sweet cloud of a specific cologne that her lead interrogator wore—something with notes of patchouli and leather. Most of the rest was gone. When she tried to deliberately recall the sequence of events—how she was taken, what they asked, how she finally got free—her mind went blank, as though a wall had been erected inside her skull. The fragments that did surface felt like scenes from a film starring someone else, a woman she almost pitied but could not claim as herself. There were gaps she could not bridge no matter how hard she concentrated.

In the months that followed, Adaeze returned to work, believing she could outrun the experience by sheer will. She was wrong. The first trigger ambushed her during a pretrial hearing. The defendant, a nervous young man, began breathing heavily as the bailiff read the charges. Adaeze felt her own chest tighten, her palms go slick. She had to call a recess, excusing herself to her chambers, where she stood gripping the edge of her desk until the sound faded from her ears. It was the same heavy, laboured breathing she had heard close to her face during the interrogation—the interrogator’s breath hot and ragged as he leaned in to whisper threats. After that, Adaeze began to notice the scent of cologne everywhere: in elevators, on colleagues, in the courtroom gallery. A lawyer’s discreet splash of something musky could make her lose the thread of argument. She started to dread the fragrance counters at department stores, stopped attending judicial conferences where handshakes and proximity were unavoidable.

The tactile trigger was the hardest to manage. Feeling physically restrained—even the light pressure of her husband’s arm across her in sleep, or the snug fit of a seatbelt during a sudden stop—sent a surge of panic through her body. She had begun to sleep on the edge of the bed, stiff and watchful, and she flinched when her husband reached for her hand in the car. He asked what was wrong; she said she was tired. She could not explain that every gentle hold brought back the rope, the helplessness, the certainty that she was about to die.

Over the following two years, Adaeze’s world narrowed. She stopped accepting invitations to social events where she could not control the environment. In court, she became more rigid, insisting on meticulous protocols and keeping her interactions with counsel brief. Her clerk noticed she would sometimes stare at a blank notepad for minutes after a particularly loud exhale from the gallery. Adaeze knew she was not the judge she used to be—the one who could read a room, pick up on subtle cues, deliver a sentence with steady conviction. Now she was constantly scanning for triggers: the sound of a deep inhale, the drift of perfume, the accidental brush of a hand. She was certain that if she let her guard down, she would fall apart, right there on the bench.

What finally brought her to seek help was a small incident that broke her resolve. During a routine proceeding, a court officer had to gently guide a distraught witness back to her seat. The officer’s hand landed on Adaeze’s shoulder for a split second—just a polite, momentary touch—and she froze, unable to speak or move. She called a recess, locked herself in her chambers, and wept. That evening, she told her husband the truth. The next day, she made an appointment with a trauma specialist. She was terrified of entering a room and recounting the gaps, the alien images, the smells that haunted her. But she was more afraid of losing everything she had built—her marriage, her career, her sense of self. She did not know if she could piece together the broken parts of the memory, but she knew she could no longer live around them, flinching at every breath and every scent.
